page_hint: §6, 'Introducing an agentic layer reshapes the system architecture in four ways:'
quoted_clause: Introducing an agentic layer reshapes the system architecture in four ways:
observed: The text announces 'four ways' but then presents seven bolded sub-headings: (1) State-management policy, (2) Inference scaling, (3) Three policies, three different levers, (4) Task economics, (5) Tool backend provisioning, (6) Observability requirements, (7) Fallback & degradation pathways. An italic sub-point ('Why agentic depth is a fleet-sizing problem') sits between (2) and (3).
evidence: Direct count of bolded items in §6. The number 'four' does not match any natural grouping of the seven items without additional restructuring.
root_cause: The section was likely expanded from an earlier four-item draft without updating the introductory count.
correction: Either change 'four ways' to 'seven ways' (or 'six ways' if 'Three policies, three different levers' is folded under 'State-management policy'), or restructure the items into four explicit groups with a brief lead-in for each group. The cleanest fix: change to 'six ways' and treat 'Three policies, three different levers' as a continuation paragraph of 'State-management policy' (remove its bold heading, make it a regular paragraph).
acceptance_test: The introductory sentence's count matches the number of bolded sub-headings that follow, or the items are explicitly grouped so the count is unambiguous.

quoted_clause: λ_step ≈ 120 ms (the model's tool-call decision step)
observed: The 120 ms is labelled 'the model's tool-call decision step' and is part of L_agent (the 'loop around the model'). However, W(T) already includes the model's prefill and decode for every invocation (Σ T_prefill + 25 ms/token × all generated tokens). If the 120 ms is model computation, it is double-counted relative to W. If it is system/scheduling overhead (queueing, context setup, kernel launch), calling it 'the model's' is misleading.
evidence: W(3) = 4.93 s prefill + 12.375 s decode + 0.399 s tool. The prefill and decode terms already account for the model reading the context and generating γ + tool-call tokens. The text explicitly states 'W already carries the per-turn model work inside the γ decode.' The 120 ms in L_agent is a separate, smaller quantity, but its physical meaning is not stated.
root_cause: The 120 ms likely represents per-invocation system overhead (scheduling, KV-cache setup, kernel launch latency) that is not captured by the idealised prefill+decode arithmetic in W, but the label 'the model's tool-call decision step' reads as model computation.
correction: Rename or re-describe λ_step. For example: 'λ_step ≈ 120 ms (per-invocation system overhead: scheduling, KV-cache slot allocation, kernel launch — not the model's FLOP time, which is in W's prefill/decode terms).' Alternatively, if it genuinely is a short model generation separate from γ, state that explicitly and show how it is not already in W's decode term.
acceptance_test: A reader can state unambiguously what physical process the 120 ms represents and confirm it is not already included in W's prefill or decode terms.

page_hint: §4, 'Multi-step reasoning cost', W formula tool leg; Table 19-1 'Tool latency (median)' row
quoted_clause: The tool/retrieval leg here uses Chapter 17's ~133 ms/turn rate; the chapter's own T·L_agent (~220 ms/turn) is the orchestration-only incremental overhead, a different quantity
observed: Two different per-turn tool rates appear: 100 ms (this chapter's λ_tool, used in L_agent and Table 19-1) and 133 ms (Ch 17's tool/retrieval rate, used in W). The text acknowledges they are 'a different quantity' and quotes Ch 17's note that 'a single model should use one rate consistently,' but never explains why the numbers differ or which components each includes.
evidence: L_agent = 120 + 100 = 220 ms. W's tool leg = 133 ms/turn. The 33 ms gap is unexplained. A reader cannot determine whether 133 ms includes retrieval/reranking that 100 ms excludes, or whether they are simply inconsistent.
root_cause: The two rates were likely derived in different chapters with slightly different scope (e.g., 100 ms = tool call only; 133 ms = tool call + vector retrieval + rerank) but the scope difference was never stated in this chapter.
correction: Add one sentence clarifying the scope difference, e.g.: 'The 100 ms here is the tool-backend round-trip (search API or SQL query); Ch 17's 133 ms additionally includes the vector-retrieval and re-rank leg that precedes the tool call in the full service-time model.' If the difference is not actually a scope difference but a rounding or estimation choice, state that and recommend unifying to one value.
acceptance_test: A reader can state what physical operations each rate (100 ms, 133 ms) covers and why they differ, without needing to open Ch 17.

quoted_clause: At the canonical workload's ~86 average in-flight requests at 10 rps (L_exec = λ × W_exec ≈ 10 × 8.6 per Ch 4; distinct from the ~100 active-user population) with the median single-turn profile (~27.2 GB/request at 10,365 tokens), the aggregate KV alone is ~86 × 27.2 GB ≈ 2.3 TB
observed: The in-flight count (86) is computed from the single-shot service time (8.6 s), but the per-request KV (27.2 GB) is from the T=1 agentic profile. If the agentic service time (W(1) ≈ 11.52 s no-reuse) were used, in-flight would be ~115 and aggregate KV ~3.1 TB. The 2.3 TB figure is therefore a lower bound, but the text does not say so.
evidence: Little's Law: L = λW. With W = 8.6 s (single-shot), L = 86. With W = 11.52 s (T=1 agentic, no-reuse), L = 115.2. The text mixes the two: 86 (from single-shot W) × 27.2 GB (from agentic T=1).
root_cause: The 86 figure is imported from Ch 4's base-system calculation. The text uses it for the agentic KV argument without noting that the agentic service time would increase the in-flight count.
correction: Add a brief qualifier: 'Using the base-system in-flight count (86, from Ch 4's 8.6 s service time) as a lower bound — the agentic T=1 service time of ~11.5 s would raise this to ~115 — the aggregate KV is already ~2.3 TB, far beyond one host's 436 GB budget.' This preserves the argument's force while being honest about the conservative estimate.
acceptance_test: The text explicitly states whether the 86 in-flight figure is a lower bound, exact, or upper bound for the agentic case, and the reader can see that the conclusion (KV >> 436 GB) is robust to the choice.

observed: The slash in '§7/§8' is non-standard for a cross-reference to two sections. It appears at least three times in §4 and once in §8.
evidence: Standard typesetting uses an en-dash (§7–§8) or 'and' (§7 and §8) for a range or pair of sections. The slash can be misread as 'section 7 or section 8.'
correction: Replace all instances of '§7/§8' with '§7–§8' (en-dash) or 'the §7 and §8 convention.'
acceptance_test: No instance of '§7/§8' remains in the chapter.

page_hint: §4, 'Tool-call latency budget', the long parenthetical after 'T is capped at 3'
quoted_clause: T is capped at 3, and the 2% fallback is a zero-added-turn single-shot for this incremental expectation — its failed-attempt work is counted unconditionally in the §8 fallback ledger
observed: This is a 35-word parenthetical embedded in a sentence that already contains a 20-word parenthetical ('conditional on a completed agent run — the §7/§8 convention; consistent with the §8 turn distribution and the §4 turn-distribution note'). The nested parentheticals make the sentence difficult to parse on first reading.
evidence: The sentence contains two em-dash parentheticals and one slash-reference, all within a single syntactic unit.
root_cause: Multiple cross-references and caveats were accumulated in one sentence rather than distributed.
correction: Break into two sentences. First: state the T cap and the conditional convention. Second: state the fallback treatment and point to §8. Example: 'T is capped at 3 (the §7–§8 conditional convention; see §8 for the turn distribution). The 2% fallback contributes zero added turns to this incremental expectation; its failed-attempt work is counted in the §8 unconditional ledger.'
acceptance_test: No sentence in the paragraph contains more than one em-dash parenthetical.

quoted_clause: On 8×H100 the per-turn agent step averages ~120 ms for a 10,000-token context
observed: The actual context length varies from 9,200 (turn 1) to 11,795 (turn 3) in the T=3 trace. '10,000' is a rounded representative value but is not flagged as such. A reader might take it as an exact threshold.
evidence: The event-level ledger shows inputs of 9,200 / 10,065 / 10,930 / 11,795. The 10,000 figure does not appear in the ledger.
root_cause: Rounding for a representative value without explicit flagging.
correction: Change to 'for a ~10,000-token context (the turn-1 input of 9,200 to the turn-3 input of 10,930 in the T=3 trace)' or simply 'for the typical per-turn context length (~9,200–11,800 tokens in the T=3 trace).'
acceptance_test: The reader can see that 10,000 is a representative value, not an exact threshold, and can map it to the actual context lengths in the ledger.

page_hint: §4, 'Per-agent-turn token amplification', the scoping note paragraph beginning 'First, a scoping note'
quoted_clause: A production agent turn is not guaranteed to be exactly 'one LLM inference + one tool call.' A turn may contain zero or more model invocations, parallel or chained tool calls, retrieval + reranking, model-generated reasoning, tool output, context compaction, or cached prefixes.
observed: This is a 120-word single paragraph that introduces the concept of an 'execution trace,' contrasts it with the simplified turn model, and states the validation requirement. It carries a lot of new terminology (execution trace, simplified execution model, token α, latency β) in one block.
evidence: The paragraph introduces: (a) the caveat about turn ≠ 1 call + 1 tool, (b) the list of what a turn may contain, (c) the 'simplified execution model' label, (d) the 'execution trace' concept, (e) the α/β framework as 'one concrete, simplified instantiation,' (f) the validation requirement.
root_cause: Multiple distinct points were compressed into one paragraph for space.
correction: Split into two or three shorter paragraphs: (1) the caveat and list of what a turn may contain; (2) the definition of 'execution trace' and how α/β relate to it; (3) the validation requirement. Alternatively, use a short callout box for the caveat and keep the execution-trace definition in the main text.
acceptance_test: No paragraph in the scoping note exceeds ~80 words, and each paragraph introduces at most two new terms.

quoted_clause: its per-token cost is ~45% lower (fewer host-hours)
observed: The stated reason for the cost difference is 'fewer host-hours' between 4 hosts (Candidate A) and 8 hosts (Candidate B). A 4:8 host ratio yields a 50% reduction in host-hours, not ~45%.
evidence: 4/8 = 0.50, so per-token cost (proportional to host-hours for the same token volume) is 50% lower. The text's own parenthetical '(fewer host-hours)' identifies the sole differentiator as host count, which gives exactly 50%, not 45%. No fixed-cost component or 8-bit-KV throughput adjustment is stated in the reasoning.
root_cause: Arithmetic error or unstated assumption. If the 45% is intentional (e.g., accounting for 8-bit KV allowing ~10% higher effective throughput per host), that reasoning is absent from the text.
correction: Change '~45% lower' to '~50% lower' to match the stated 'fewer host-hours' reasoning (4 vs 8 hosts). Alternatively, if 45% is the intended figure, add the missing reasoning: e.g., '(fewer host-hours; the 8-bit KV also raises per-host effective throughput by ~10%, narrowing the gap slightly)'.
acceptance_test: The per-token cost reduction stated in the text must equal (1 − hosts_A/hosts_B) when the sole stated differentiator is host count, or the text must explicitly state the additional factor that moves the figure from 50% to 45%.

page_hint: Ch 22, Figure 22.1 note, 'Prefill is compute-bound' sentence
quoted_clause: ~1.19 PFLOPS required at the ~1.08 s budget
observed: The 1.08 s prefill time budget is used in the rate calculation (1.29/1.08 = 1.19 PFLOPS) but is neither derived in this chapter nor explicitly cross-referenced to its source. The reader encounters it as a given.
evidence: The TTFT SLO is 2 s (p95, Ch 4). The 1.08 s appears to be the prefill component of that budget after subtracting queueing, network, and first-token time, but the decomposition is not shown here. The figure note uses it without a parenthetical like '(Ch 8 §X: prefill allocation from the 2 s TTFT budget)'.
root_cause: The number is likely established in Ch 8 or Ch 14, but the cross-reference is implicit rather than explicit at the point of use.
correction: Add a brief parenthetical at first use: '(~1.08 s prefill allocation from the 2 s TTFT budget, Ch 8 §X)' or similar, so the reader can trace the number without flipping to another chapter.
acceptance_test: A reader encountering the 1.08 s figure for the first time can identify, from the text at that location, which chapter/section establishes it and what the full TTFT decomposition is.

quoted_clause: The reasoning is traced by the architect and the system investigating together.
observed: The phrase 'the system investigating together' is ambiguous. It could mean (a) the book's reasoning framework, (b) the deployed system under design, or (c) the architect and the system co-investigating. In context the intended meaning is (a), but the sentence reads as if the system is an agent.
evidence: The preceding sentence says 'We do not reach for vendor marketing numbers or rule-of-thumb heuristics. Instead we trace a vague stakeholder ask... through a canonical loop.' The 'system' here most naturally refers to the loop/framework, but the sentence structure makes it read as a co-investigator.
root_cause: Vague noun reference in a transitional sentence.
correction: Rewrite for clarity, e.g., 'The reasoning is traced by the architect using the canonical loop as a structured investigation framework.' Or simply delete the sentence if the preceding paragraph already conveys the point.
acceptance_test: A reader can identify unambiguously what 'the system' refers to without re-reading the paragraph.

quoted_clause: A100 (and the 8×H100 host) natively supports BF16 and TF32 on its Tensor Cores.
observed: The pronoun 'its' is ambiguous: it could refer to A100 (singular) or the 8×H100 host (collective). The technical point (both GPUs support BF16 natively) is correct, but the sentence structure creates a momentary parse ambiguity.
evidence: A100 is a single GPU; 'the 8×H100 host' is a multi-GPU system. 'Its Tensor Cores' most naturally attaches to the nearest singular noun (A100), but the parenthetical includes the H100 host as well.
root_cause: Sentence structure with a parenthetical that changes the referent.
correction: Rewrite: 'Both A100 and H100 natively support BF16 and TF32 on their Tensor Cores; no next-generation GPU is required.'
acceptance_test: The sentence unambiguously attributes BF16/TF32 support to both GPU types without a dangling pronoun.

quoted_clause: the canonical ~2,000-user, ~10 rps / ~40 rps peak, RAG Q&A, 70B dense FP16 scenario that every other chapter in this handbook cites
observed: 'Every other chapter' is a universal claim. It is plausible that most chapters reference the canonical scenario, but 'every' is strong and may not be literally true (e.g., a chapter on ADR format or red-team methodology might not cite the specific numbers).
evidence: Without the full manuscript, I cannot verify that literally every chapter cites the canonical scenario. The intent is clear (the scenario is the book's through-line), but the universal quantifier is a small overstatement risk.
root_cause: Rhetorical emphasis ('every') slightly exceeding the verifiable claim.
correction: Soften to 'the canonical... scenario that the handbook's chapters cite throughout' or 'that most chapters in this handbook reference.'
acceptance_test: The claim is either verifiably true for every chapter, or the wording is softened to match the actual coverage.

page_hint: Ch 24 §3.3, 'Red Team runs the adversarial pass', item 1
observed: 40 × 1.29 = 51.6, not 51.5. The text displays 1.29 (rounded from 1.288) but computes with 1.288 (40 × 1.288 = 51.52 ≈ 51.5). The displayed multiplication is internally inconsistent at the shown precision.
evidence: 1.29 × 40 = 51.6. 1.288 × 40 = 51.52. The text writes '40 ×1.29 PFLOP ≈ 51.5 PFLOP/s', which a reader checking the arithmetic would find off by 0.1.
root_cause: Display rounding (1.29) vs. working precision (1.288) mismatch in the shown equation.
correction: Either write '40 × 1.288 PFLOP ≈ 51.5 PFLOP/s' (using the unrounded value in the displayed equation) or write '40 × 1.29 PFLOP ≈ 51.6 PFLOP/s' (using the rounded value consistently). The former is preferable since 51.5 is the value used downstream.
acceptance_test: A reader who multiplies the two displayed numbers (40 and 1.29) gets a result consistent with the displayed product (within the shown rounding).

page_hint: Ch 22 Table 22-1 and Ch 24 §3.3 vs. Ch 25 mini-case
observed: The same concept (8-bit floating-point KV cache) is labeled '8-bit KV' in Ch 22 and Ch 24 but 'FP8 KV' in Ch 25. While the context always makes clear it is floating-point (byte-halving of FP16), the terminology shift is a minor inconsistency that could confuse a reader scanning across chapters.
evidence: Ch 22: 'at 8-bit KV the same 9.2K context falls to ~12.06 GB'. Ch 24: 'Candidate A: 4×H100 hosts, 8-bit KV'. Ch 25: 'Render the KV cache in FP8 for the long-context decode path.' All refer to the same 1.31 MB/token format.
root_cause: Terminology drift across chapters written at different times.
correction: Standardize on 'FP8 KV' throughout (more precise, distinguishes from INT8), or use '8-bit (FP8) KV' at first mention in each chapter and 'FP8 KV' thereafter. The house convention lists 'FP8/INT8/8-bit' as a check item.
acceptance_test: A global search for '8-bit KV' and 'FP8 KV' returns a consistent usage pattern (one primary term, the other only as a first-mention gloss).
